dedupe_keys.name: ports and environmental justice in the united states a screening of 50 ports with ejscreen

description: This study by Michael Greenberg of Rutgers University, published in Risk Analysis in 2021, is a screening environmental justice analysis of the 50 United States ports that each handle more than 10 million tons of products. Coverage: seven demographic and 11 environmental metrics from the US EPA EJSCREEN tool, compared at distances of 2, 5 and 10 miles from each port centroid. The 2-mile zones had higher values for 13 of the 18 environmental inequity indicators, including all three measures of air toxics, fine particles, proximity to hazardous waste sites and to facilities with risk management plans, and indicators of low socioeconomic status and minority populations. The author discusses the need to maintain and upgrade the EPA screening tool and how port neighbourhoods' futures depend on civic groups, elected officials, port authorities and port users. Format and access: a journal article; the abstract is public on PubMed. Licence and cost: closed access, paid. Caveats: a screening with fixed distance rings around port centroids, not a dose or exposure model; the abstract was read, not the full text. The distance-ring approach and indicator set can define equity weights for port expansion and hazard exposure scenarios. It relates to the Port of Oakland environmental justice systems analysis and the Port of Mobile vulnerability study in the catalogue.
